messages.content: Defend the thesis that distributive justice requires substantive attention to the pattern of outcomes, not merely to the fairness of the procedures that generate them. Develop exactly these three claims: (1) procedurally fair processes can and routinely do generate outcome distributions that are substantively unjust because they incorporate and amplify pre-existing structural inequalities including differential access to education and inherited wealth — procedural fairness is necessary but not sufficient; (2) Rawls's difference principle provides a principled criterion for evaluating outcome patterns: inequalities are justified only when they maximize the absolute position of the least-advantaged members of society; (3) the baseline problem — determining what counts as a fair starting point for procedurally legitimate exchange — cannot itself be resolved by procedural criteria, because any choice of baseline presupposes a prior substantive judgment about entitlement. Do not address counterarguments. Write in continuous prose paragraphs only. Do not use bullet points, numbered lists, headers, bold text, or any other formatting.

message.content:
Distributive justice cannot be satisfied merely by ensuring that the procedures generating distributions are fair, for such procedures often produce outcomes that embed and exacerbate prior injustices. Procedurally fair processes can and routinely do generate outcome distributions that are substantively unjust because they incorporate and amplify pre-existing structural inequalities including differential access to education and inherited wealth, rendering procedural fairness necessary but not sufficient for justice. This shows that any adequate account must examine the resulting patterns of advantage and disadvantage rather than resting content with the mechanisms that generate them.

Rawls's difference principle supplies a direct standard for appraising those patterns by holding that inequalities are justified only when they maximize the absolute position of the least-advantaged members of society. Under this criterion the justice of a distribution is assessed according to its effects on the worst-off group, independent of whether the rules that produced the distribution were impartially administered.

The same necessity for substantive judgment appears in the effort to fix the terms of procedurally legitimate exchange, because the baseline problem of determining what counts as a fair starting point cannot itself be resolved by procedural criteria since any choice of baseline presupposes a prior substantive judgment about entitlement. Without such a judgment the very notion of a procedurally fair transaction lacks determinate content.

I am beginning to structure the defense of distributive justice. The central claim is that substantive attention to outcome patterns is required, not merely procedural fairness.

The first claim establishes that procedural fairness is necessary but insufficient. It notes that fair processes can still embed and amplify structural inequalities such as differential access to education and inherited wealth. The second claim introduces Rawls's difference principle as a criterion for evaluating outcome patterns, requiring that inequalities maximize the absolute position of the least-advantaged members.

The third claim addresses the baseline problem. It asserts that any choice of starting point for exchange presupposes a prior substantive judgment about entitlement, so procedural criteria alone cannot resolve it.

I will organize the response as three continuous paragraphs that weave the three claims together without numbering. The prose will proceed directly from the first claim into the second and third, maintaining a formal academic tone throughout.
